note: Corpus for playlist.json. Two shelves and a ledger. The LISTENING shelf is curation — my picks, and the choice of room is opinion, stated as opinion. Only the facts were verified: every track was checked against MusicBrainz in batches (one search per track, to stay inside a free service's one-request-per-second etiquette), and the checkers were told to report exactly what I had got wrong rather than silently fix it. The PLAYABLE shelf is different in kind: music whose licence was read on the page that states it, which this house could legally put behind a room. The LEDGER applies the verified licensing rule to ten promises the house already made and never kept.
method: artbitrage playlist-verify workflow, 8 agents: 6 batched MusicBrainz identity checks, 2 licence researchers. 23 of 24 tracks confirmed, 1 dropped as non-existent, 3 artist credits corrected.
curation_is_opinion: Which tracks are here, and which room each one sits in, is one person's taste and one person's joke. None of it is a finding. The facts underneath — that a recording exists, under that exact artist credit, in that year — are the only part that was checked.
no_audio_hosted: Artbitrage hosts none of the listening shelf, streams none of it, and grants no rights in any of it. Each entry links to MusicBrainz, which is an open catalogue of facts about music, not a place to hear it. Take the titles to whatever service you already use.
no_lyrics: No lyric from any of these songs appears anywhere in this room or its data, by design.

listening.title: Are You With Me
listening.why_this_room: The whole house in one track. It is a rework of a country song — Easton Corbin, 2012 — moved onto a dance floor. Art as arbitrage, literally: same song, different market, and the gap between them is where the value appeared.
listening.fact_notes: Cover: the song was originally recorded by American country singer Easton Corbin (2012, album 'All Over the Road'), written by Terry McBride, Shane McAnally and Josh Osborne. Lost Frequencies' version is a remix/rework of that recording. Earliest release date visible in the response: 2014-08-01.

licensing_findings.title: FINDING: every piece of recorded classical music carries (at least) two copyrights — the work and the recording
licensing_findings.license: n/a — legal finding, not a licence
licensing_findings.suits: The core rule for anyone putting a Gymnopédie behind a web page: Satie's COMPOSITION has been public domain worldwide for decades (he died 1925, life+70 expired 1996), but every RECORDING of it has its own separate copyright belonging to the performer/producer. Musopen's own FAQ states it plainly: 'there are at least two copyrights to any sound recording of a musical work — the copyright on the underlying composition and the copyright on the particular performance', and 'Although certain musical compositions may be in the public domain, a particular recording of the musical composition may remain under copyright protection.' Cornell's chart carries the same warning: its sound-recording table 'applies only to the sound recording itself, and not to any copyrights in underlying compositions.' Practical consequence: you may not rip a Ciccolini or de Leeuw Gymnopédie from a CD or YouTube — you need a recording whose OWN rights are PD/CC0/CC-licensed (items 1 and 2 above), or you record it yourself.
licensing_findings.cannot_establish: Nothing material — this is black-letter law confirmed by two independent fetched sources.

licensing_findings.title: FINDING: US sound-recording terms (Music Modernization Act) — almost no famous 20th-century classical recording is PD in the US
licensing_findings.suits: The US schedule under the Classics Protection and Access Act: recordings first published before 1923 entered the public domain at the end of 2021; 1923–1946 recordings get 95+5 = 100 years from publication; 1947–1956 get 95+15 = 110 years; everything else fixed before 15 Feb 1972 is protected until 15 February 2067. So the celebrated mid-century Satie/Bach/Chopin recordings (1950s–60s labels) stay copyrighted in the US for decades yet — only acoustic-era (pre-1923) recordings, with period sound quality, are safely PD-by-age today.
licensing_findings.cannot_establish: Post-1972 recordings follow ordinary federal terms (typically 95 years from publication for works-made-for-hire) — not detailed on this page; check the Cornell chart per recording.

licensing_findings.title: FINDING: UK/EU phonogram term — 70 years from publication, extension did NOT revive expired recordings
licensing_findings.suits: GOV.UK, verbatim: sound and music recordings are protected '70 years from when it's first published' (compositions: 70 years after the author's death). The 70 came from Directive 2011/77/EU, which raised the term from 50 and applies only to recordings 'still protected... as at 1 November 2013' — expired rights were not revived. Net effect: recordings published before 1963 are out of phonogram copyright in the UK/EU (which is why early-'60s recordings circulate freely in Europe) — but the SAME recordings can remain copyrighted in the US until the 2030s–2067 (previous item). A geo-agnostic public web page should satisfy the stricter US rule. Where to check: gov.uk/copyright for the UK, EUR-Lex 2011/77/EU for the EU, copyright.gov for the US.
licensing_findings.cannot_establish: Whether performers' 'equitable remuneration' for public performance/communication in some EU states could touch a website playing even a licence-cleared recording — that is a collecting-society question outside what these pages state; PD/CC0 dedications like items 1–2 waive related rights, which is the clean path.

licensing_findings.title: FINDING: what Musopen actually is — an uploader-warranted PD repository plus commissioned PD recordings, with no review of uploads
licensing_findings.license: per-recording: mostly public-domain dedications, some Creative Commons; verify each file
licensing_findings.attribution_string: per recording — PD items need none; CC items need the performer credited per their licence
licensing_findings.suits: Musopen (501(c)(3), founded 2006, 'to set music free') has two kinds of content. (1) Recordings it COMMISSIONED for release: the 2010 Kickstarter ($68,359) hired the Czech Philharmonic for Beethoven/Brahms/Tchaikovsky/Sibelius, and the 2013 one (~$90k) funded the complete works of Chopin — these were made to be freed. (2) USER UPLOADS, which dominate the catalogue: the FAQ says uploaders must 'represent and warrant that content uploaded to the site is in the public domain', but — verbatim — 'Musopen cannot guarantee that any music uploaded by its users is, in fact, in the public domain' and 'Musopen does not review music uploaded by users of the site.' It is a freemium service (5 free downloads/day; ~$55/yr for HD), but the money buys bandwidth, not the licence. Verdict: a genuinely good source, but the licence lives on each recording's page, not on the site — read it per file, and keep a copy.
licensing_findings.cannot_establish: The live site returns 403 to non-browser fetchers (Cloudflare), so the FAQ quoted is the Nov 2020 archived version; whether individual catalogue pages today also carry CC BY-NC labels on some tracks could not be confirmed this session — treat any Musopen track without an explicit PD/CC statement as unusable until checked.

licensing_findings.title: TRAP: Content ID claims genuinely public-domain music — and the claimant does not always back down
licensing_findings.artist: documented in Wikipedia's Content ID article
licensing_findings.suits: Fetched, documented cases: in 2018 a German professor uploaded recordings of compositions whose composers had been dead over 70 years — Deutsche Grammophon refused to lift two claims even after he demonstrated public-domain status; the same year a video of pure white noise drew copyright notices. Content ID matches audio fingerprints with no human review for PD status, and labels have fingerprinted their own recordings of PD works — so a rights-holder's claim on YOUR page's PD/CC0 audio (or on a video containing it) is a routine hazard, not a sign you did something wrong. Defence for a site builder: keep the licence page (archived copy) and provenance chain for every file you serve, so a claim or a DMCA notice can be answered with evidence the same day.
licensing_findings.cannot_establish: The frequently-cited 2018 James Rhodes case (Sony claiming 47 seconds of his own Bach performance on Facebook, withdrawn after public outcry) is consistent with this pattern but was NOT verifiable this session — Ars Technica is unfetchable from here and his Wikipedia article omits it — so I report it as unconfirmed.

licensing_findings.title: TRAP: 'royalty-free' is a commercial licence category, not 'free' — and never public domain
licensing_findings.artist: Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) as the worked example
licensing_findings.license: n/a — cautionary finding (MacLeod's own catalogue: CC BY 4.0, or a paid Standard License to skip attribution)
licensing_findings.attribution_string: if using MacLeod's music the required form is: "[Title]" Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), Licensed under Creative Commons: By Attribution 4.0
licensing_findings.suits: 'Royalty-free' means only 'no per-use royalties after you obtain the licence' — the music stays copyrighted, and at most stock libraries the licence itself costs money and forbids redistribution. The honest end of the spectrum is Kevin MacLeod: his FAQ confirms the music is free to use under CC BY 4.0 with mandatory, findable credit (exact string above), with a PAID licence only for cases where attribution is impossible. Relevant here: the polished 'Gymnopedie No. 2' floating around the free-music world (including on Wikimedia Commons, ISRC USUAN1100786) is MacLeod's CC BY recording — usable on a commercial site, but only WITH the credit line. Rule of thumb: 'royalty-free' on a download site tells you nothing about your rights; only the named licence (CC0, CC BY, CC BY-NC, paid EULA) does — and any 'NC' kills use on a commercial page.
licensing_findings.cannot_establish: Nothing material for MacLeod (terms fetched); terms of other 'royalty-free' stock libraries vary per vendor and were not individually reviewed.

promise_ledger.why: Nobody holds a composition right in a paleolithic melody. A modern reconstruction is a performance, so the recording has its own rights — find one released CC0 or CC BY, or record one.

promise_ledger.promised: a reconstructed chant recorded in Chartres or Notre Dame
promise_ledger.why: Plainchant is centuries out of copyright. A modern critical edition can carry editorial rights and the recording certainly does, so the job is finding a freely licensed performance, not clearing the music.

promise_ledger.promised: a Palestrina motet or a Josquin des Prez chanson
promise_ledger.why: Both composers died in the 16th century. Compositions long free; only the recording needs clearing.

promise_ledger.promised: Bach's Toccata and Fugue in D minor (BWV 565) on a Baroque organ
promise_ledger.why: Bach died in 1750. And there is already a verified CC0 Bach recording on the playable shelf — Kimiko Ishizaka's Open Goldberg Variations. Different work, different instrument, but it proves the path exists.

promise_ledger.promised: the Ninth Symphony's choral finale, or Chopin's Nocturne Op. 9 No. 2
promise_ledger.why: Beethoven died 1827, Chopin 1849. This is the best-supported promise of the ten: Musopen crowdfunded a complete Chopin recording specifically to release it freely.

promise_ledger.promised: the Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune opening, or a synthesized whole-tone scale
promise_ledger.why: Debussy died in 1918, so the composition is free. The second option is better still: a whole-tone scale generated in the browser has no recording to clear at all.

promise_ledger.promised: a clip from the Sacrificial Dance, or a Schoenberg atonal fragment
promise_ledger.why: The Rite of Spring cannot be used. Stravinsky died in 1971, so in the UK and EU his compositions stay in copyright until the end of 2041 — the composition itself, before any recording. Schoenberg died in 1951 and is free in the UK/EU. Keep the promise by swapping to Schoenberg and saying why.

promise_ledger.promised: a curated pop single from the era, or a generated piece using Pop Art's principles
promise_ledger.why: A 1960s pop single is squarely in copyright in every jurisdiction that matters, in both the song and the recording. The second half of the same note is fully keepable: a generated piece has nothing to clear.
A field recording. Either make it — a phone and a cork is the whole production — or take a CC0 one from a sound library.

promise_ledger.promised: a factory lector reading over the rolling floor
promise_ledger.why: A living tradition, so a recording of it belongs to whoever made it and arguably to the lector. Archival recordings carry their own rights. This one needs permission, not a licence search.

builder_notes: How this was done, and what to know before wiring audio in. (1) The session's web-search budget was already exhausted (200/200), so every finding came from direct page fetches of known catalogues plus the Internet Archive's advancedsearch JSON API (collection:netlabels, subject:ambient, licenseurl by/4.0) — that API is how the two netlabel albums were found. (2) Dead ends: sessions.blue/license 404s (the real page is /licensing); FMA's Chris Zabriskie pages 404 under both slug styles, so he was dropped despite being CC BY 4.0 elsewhere; FMA's /music/Meydn/ 404s but /music/Meydan/ works; Incompetech's /licenses/ page renders without naming a CC version — the version (CC BY 4.0) is stated on his FAQ page, which was fetched. (3) Licence ambiguities found and resolved by reading the actual pages: FMA labels Kevin MacLeod's album 'Attribution 3.0 International' while Incompetech's own FAQ grants CC BY 4.0 with an exact credit format — use the 4.0 credit line; Archive.org search metadata said Aquatone was plain BY 4.0 but the item page says BY-SA 4.0 — always trust the item page; FMA album pages sometimes say 'check individual tracks' (Kai Engel's 'Idea' does), so licences must be verified per track, which I did for every item above. (4) Blue Dot Sessions is the only NC item: their mp3s are CC BY-NC 4.0, free with attribution for non-monetized, not-part-of-your-job projects — fine for this site today, a problem the day it monetizes. Everything else is CC0, CC BY (2.5/3.0/4.0) or BY-SA 4.0 — no ND anywhere, as asked. (5) Builder practicalities: self-host the audio files rather than hotlinking FMA/archive.org (both throttle and reorganize URLs); put the attribution line visibly near the player or on a linked credits page (CC BY requires it); keep a dated copy or screenshot of each licence page, since FMA has changed owners twice and pages move; ccMixter is plain http. (6) What no fetch can establish: a CC licence is only as good as the uploader's right to grant it — none of these pages prove chain of title, though all are long-standing moderated catalogues. (7) Mood caveat: licences were verified by fetching; tempo/mood mostly from tags and descriptions, not ears — audition Komiku (chiptune-flavoured) and Grove of Whispers (dark drone) before committing. Do not reproduce lyrics anywhere; all recommended tracks are instrumental.

HOW THIS WAS RESEARCHED: the session's WebSearch budget was already exhausted (200/200, shared across the workflow), so every fact above comes from direct fetches of known primary sources — nothing is from memory alone except where explicitly flagged unconfirmed. DEAD ENDS: musopen.org serves a Cloudflare 'Just a moment...' challenge to both WebFetch and curl-with-browser-UA (403), so its FAQ was read from the Wayback Machine snapshot of 2020-11-27 (web.archive.org is blocked for WebFetch but reachable via curl; the CDX API confirmed the snapshot is a real 200 capture). Kickstarter also 403s; Ars Technica is unfetchable (so the James Rhodes/Sony Bach story stays UNCONFIRMED — do not cite it as fact without a source); the Creative Commons wiki case-study page for Musopen is a 404. Cornell's chart summary came back slightly garbled on the pre-1923 boundary — use copyright.gov (fetched, quoted) as the anchor for US recording terms. WHAT THE BUILDER MUST KNOW BEFORE PUTTING AUDIO BEHIND A PAGE: (1) clear BOTH rights — composition (composer) AND recording (performer/producer); for Satie/Bach/Chopin the composition side is done, the recording side is the whole job. (2) The two safest concrete files found: the Robin Alciatore Gymnopédie No. 1 (PD, on Wikimedia Commons with a direct upload.wikimedia.org URL — but self-host a copy rather than hotlinking; Commons files can be renamed/deleted) and Kimiko Ishizaka's Open Goldberg Variations (CC0; note her Bandcamp page's machine licence line contradictorily shows CC BY 4.0 while the description and official site say CC0 — crediting her resolves the ambiguity in practice). (3) Archive the licence page of every file you serve (screenshot + saved HTML) the day you adopt it — that is your answer to a future Content ID or DMCA claim on genuinely PD audio. (4) Jurisdiction: UK/EU frees recordings published before 1963; the US does not (until 2033+ / 2067) — a public site should satisfy the US rule, i.e., use PD-DEDICATED or CC0/CC BY recordings, not merely old ones. (5) 'Royalty-free' and 'free to listen' are not licences; any NC clause is fatal for a commercial page. (6) Wikimedia Commons 'own work' PD/CC0 claims (like the anonymous-performer 'Gymnopedie No. 1..ogg', CC0) ultimately rest on the uploader's honesty — prefer files with a named performer and a traceable source, as in the two items above.
